To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the native wheatgrass and wildrye grasses tested in our study did not accumulate heavy metals in sufficient quantities to be useful in a phytoremediation program.
native wheatgrasses, wildryes, and other grass species have the potential to be used as phytoremediation materials in the future.
none of the native grasses evaluated in this study were suitable for phytoextraction of Al, As, Cd, Cr, Cu, Fe Mn, Ni, and Zn.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of native WG and WR that possess a broad adaptability to ecological sites and have the ability to exclude and uptake heavy metals of concern.
the identification and characterization of native plant species for use in phytoremediation of heavy metals on abandoned mine land in western Montana.
the identification of native plant species that are adapted to the soils of western Montana that have the potential to exclude or accumulate specific heavy metals of interest in the soil.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
no native WG and WR species were found to be hyperaccumulator species for any metal tested in this study.
none of the native WG and WR cultivars/ germplasms tested in this study could be used as hyperaccumulator species for Al, Ar, Cr, Cu, Fe.
none of the species tested in this study could be used as hyperaccumulators for the metals of interest.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
native plants are a potential source of forage for wildlife, but not as a hyperaccumulator species for the metals studied.
none of the native WG and WR studied have the potential to be used in phyto extraction programs for the removal of As, Cr, Cu, Fe and Pb from mine tailings soils in western Montana.
none of the native WG and WR cultivars/ germplasms studied are hyperaccumulators for any of the heavy metals tested.
The main takeaway from our work is that
native WG and WR species are not suitable for phytoextraction purposes due to their inability to extract metals from soil.
the native WG and WR species studied were not hyperaccumulators for the metals tested and therefore are not good candidates for phytoextraction of these metals.
native plants can be grown on metal-contaminated soils and still provide forage for livestock and wildlife.
